info.name: ThunderID - M2M Application Sharing Across Organization Units
info.description:
End-to-end demo of a machine-to-machine service that serves many organization units from one credential pair, without being visible inside any of them.

A token is requested against a named organization unit via POST /ou/{ouId}/oauth2/token. Three separate organization units are involved in answering that request:

- the accessing OU decides whether the application may be used at all (its grant),
- the application's own owning OU decides what the application is entitled to (its roles and group memberships),
- the accessing OU then narrows what the token may actually carry (its resource grants).

Omitting the /ou/{ouId} prefix keeps the pre-existing behaviour exactly: no grant is consulted, no scope filtering happens, and the claims stay with the application's owner.

Application sharing is declarative-only by design; there is no REST API for it. Run the setup guide in README.md before this collection.

item.name: 00 - Setup
item.description: Obtains the admin token every management request in this collection uses, and confirms the declaratively defined organization units and M2M applications are present. Application grants have no REST API by design, so those three applications must come from declarative YAML: see the README's setup guide. Run this folder first.

item.name: 03 - allChildren Grant: The Owning Subtree
item.description: decl-m2m-subtree declares `grants: [- allChildren: true]`: every organization unit beneath its owner, any depth, including ones created later. It stops at the subtree boundary.

request.description: A child of the owning organization unit is covered by the blanket subtree grant.

item.name: NEGATIVE: Token for Another Root's Child

request.description: The grant is anchored at the application's own organization unit, so it reaches downward from there and nowhere else. A child in a different tree is refused exactly as its root was, which is what proves allChildren is a subtree scope rather than a 'any descendant anywhere' one.

item.name: 04 - Selective Grant: Named Organization Units Only
item.description: decl-m2m-selective declares `grants: [- ouIds: [decl-m2m-child-a]]`. This is the case the whole feature exists for: two sibling organization units in the same subtree, only one of which the service may serve.

item.name: Token for Child A (Named in the Grant)

request.description: The one organization unit the grant names.

item.name: NEGATIVE: Token for Child B (Sibling, Not Named)

request.description: Child B sits in the same subtree as child A and differs only in not being named by the grant. Being a sibling of a granted organization unit confers nothing.

item.name: Owner Needs No Grant of Its Own

request.description: The owning organization unit may always name itself, without appearing in any grant.

item.name: 05 - Negative: Unresolvable and Unauthenticated
item.description: Failure modes that are not about grants: an organization unit id that resolves to nothing, and a bad client secret. The accessing organization unit is resolved before its grant is consulted, so an unknown id is refused even under a blanket allOus grant, which would otherwise match any string.

item.name: NEGATIVE: Unknown OU Under a Selective Grant

request.description: An organization unit the application has no grant for, which also happens not to exist.

item.name: NEGATIVE: Unknown OU Under an allOus Grant

request.description: The interesting half: allOus means every organization unit in the deployment, and a grant check alone can never reject an id that names none of them. Resolving the organization unit before consulting the grant is what makes this a clean refusal rather than a 500.
Client authentication runs before any organization unit logic, so a bad secret fails as invalid_client regardless of how well granted the application is.

item.name: 06 - Scope Filtering by the Accessing Organization Unit
item.description: Builds a resource server with two resources, entitles the service to all of it through a role in its own organization unit, then grants the server to a child while withholding one resource. The same credential then yields different scopes depending on which organization unit the token is requested against. Everything here is API-creatable; only the application grants are declarative.

request.description: A resource server owned by the same organization unit that owns the M2M applications. Its permissions are what the scope filter will later narrow.

item.name: Create Role in the Owning OU, Assigned to the Service

request.description: The application's entitlement lives in its own owning organization unit. This role carries every permission and is assigned directly to the subtree-granted application. Nothing about it varies per accessing organization unit.

item.name: Scopes for Child A (Narrowed to What Was Granted)

request.description: The point of the feature. Same credential, same role, same requested scopes: the token is narrower because the child was never granted the orders resource. Entitlement is resolved from the application's owning organization unit; what the token may carry is then filtered by what the accessing organization unit can actually see.
